title: Ethiopian Organ Meat Mix
community: All of Ethiopia — the offal dish of celebration and nothing wasted
author: Chef Haile
desc: Ethiopian Dulet — a mixture of minced raw or lightly cooked beef tripe, liver, and lean beef, seasoned with mitmita, jalapeño, onion, and kibbeh. The offal celebration dish — eaten at feasts where whole animals are slaughtered, honouring the animal completely and wasting nothing.
longDesc: Dulet is the Ethiopian philosophy of whole-animal eating made into a dish — when a cattle or sheep is slaughtered for a celebration, the organs are mixed with lean meat, seasoned with mitmita and jalapeño, and eaten as a celebration in themselves. Nothing is discarded; everything is honoured.
ingredients: 200g beef or lamb tripe — cleaned and finely minced
150g beef or lamb liver — finely minced or chopped
steps: Combine all three meats with onion, jalapeño, garlic, and salt.
Add meat mixture. Cook, stirring, 5—8 minutes.
Dulet can be served raw (leb-leb) or cooked through.
chefTips: The freshest possible organ meats are essential.
The balance of tripe, liver, and lean beef is traditional — each contributes differently.
Cook to your preferred level — many eat dulet leb-leb (slightly warmed but not fully cooked).
cookingScience: Liver contains extremely high concentrations of B12, iron, and vitamin A — these nutrients are heat-labile to varying degrees. Lightly cooking (leb-leb) preserves more of these nutrients than fully cooking. Tripe's collagen partially dissolves even in brief cooking, releasing gelatin that gives dulet its characteristic slightly sticky consistency.
sustainabilityTips: Dulet is whole-animal eating at its most complete — the zero-waste philosophy of Ethiopian celebration cooking.
storage: Eat immediately — no storage for raw. Cooked: refrigerate 2 days.
healthBenefits: Liver: the world's most nutrient-dense food.
culturalNote: Dulet is the dish of wholeness — the celebration that honours the entire animal, the acknowledgment that every part of what was sacrificed deserves respect. In Ethiopian celebration cooking, nothing from a slaughtered animal is discarded.
